candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.7 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'It is expedient (sympherei) for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send Him unto you' Cyril takes as the dominical pneumatology of progressive economy. Christ's bodily departure is necessary for the Spirit's coming because the modes of presence are different: Christ in the flesh was geographically limited (could be in one place at a time); the Spirit indwelling the Church is universally present everywhere His people gather. The 'expedient' (sympherei — beneficial / advantageous) Cyril emphasizes as not consolation-prize but actual upgrade: ascension + Spirit-coming is a richer mode of presence than incarnate proximity. The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this Cyrilline reading.

'Turned' (genēsetai eis charan — shall be made into joy) Cyril takes literally: not 'replaced by' joy after sorrow ends, but TRANSFORMED INTO joy. Cyril applies this to every subsequent Christian experience of suffering: nothing in the Christian life is finally lost; every present sorrow is the seed of a future joy by participation in the paschal pattern. candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.28 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father' Cyril takes as the compressed Johannine summary of the entire incarnational economy. The four-fold movement (procession from Father / incarnation into world / departure from world / return to Father) Cyril reads as the dogmatic structure that the entire Gospel of John traces verse-by-verse. The 'came forth' (exēlthon) preserves the eternal procession; the 'come into the world' (elēlytha eis ton kosmon) marks the historical incarnation; the 'leave the world' (aphiēmi ton kosmon) anticipates the cross-and-ascension; the 'go to the Father' (poreuomai pros ton Patera) marks the consummation in glory. The Tewahedo Christmas Anaphora explicitly echoes all four movements.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.33 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:

'In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome (nenikēka) the world' is for Cyril the closing dominical pin of the Farewell Discourses. The perfect tense 'have overcome' (nenikēka — completed action with continuing result) Cyril takes proleptically: the victory is spoken of as already accomplished from the perspective of the eternal Word, even though the cross-and-resurrection still lay ahead historically. 'Be of good cheer' (tharseite — take courage, be confident) is therefore not consolation despite-defeat but participatory rejoicing-in-victory: the disciples are invited to share Christ's confidence that the outcome is settled. This grounds the Tewahedo martyrological tradition's characteristic theological confidence.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'It is expedient (sympherei) for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send Him unto you' Cyril takes as the dominical pneumatology of progressive economy. Christ's bodily departure is necessary for the Spirit's coming because the modes of presence are different: Christ in the flesh was geographically limited (could be in one place at a time); the Spirit indwelling the Church is universally present everywhere His people gather. The 'expedient' (sympherei — beneficial / advantageous) Cyril emphasizes as not consolation-prize but actual upgrade: ascension + Spirit-coming is a richer mode of presence than incarnate proximity. The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this Cyrilline reading.

'When He, the Spirit of truth, is come, He will guide you into all truth: for He shall not speak of Himself; but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak' Cyril unpacks against any reading that would make the Spirit a separate or supplementary teaching source. 'He shall not speak of Himself' Cyril reads as expressing perfect Trinitarian harmony: the Spirit's teaching IS the Father's + Son's teaching, mediated through the Spirit's distinctive operation, not a separate revelation. 'All truth' (eis tēn alētheian pasan) Cyril limits to the Christological-soteriological deposit: the Spirit guides into ALL the truth Christ has given, not into endless new revelations. This grounds patristic-Tewahedo apostolic-deposit doctrine.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy' Cyril reads as the eschatological pattern of Christian experience: present suffering is not negated but transmuted by the resurrection. 'Turned' (genēsetai eis charan — shall be made into joy) Cyril takes literally: not 'replaced by' joy after sorrow ends, but TRANSFORMED INTO joy. The Easter pattern (Friday's sorrow becomes Sunday's joy through the cross-resurrection event) is the paradigm. Cyril applies this to every subsequent Christian experience of suffering: nothing in the Christian life is finally lost; every present sorrow is the seed of a future joy by participation in the paschal pattern. The Tewahedo Easter Anaphora preserves this transformative reading.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father' Cyril takes as the compressed Johannine summary of the entire incarnational economy. The four-fold movement (procession from Father / incarnation into world / departure from world / return to Father) Cyril reads as the dogmatic structure that the entire Gospel of John traces verse-by-verse. The 'came forth' (exēlthon) preserves the eternal procession; the 'come into the world' (elēlytha eis ton kosmon) marks the historical incarnation; the 'leave the world' (aphiēmi ton kosmon) anticipates the cross-and-ascension; the 'go to the Father' (poreuomai pros ton Patera) marks the consummation in glory. The Tewahedo Christmas Anaphora explicitly echoes all four movements.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome (nenikēka) the world' is for Cyril the closing dominical pin of the Farewell Discourses. The perfect tense 'have overcome' (nenikēka — completed action with continuing result) Cyril takes proleptically: the victory is spoken of as already accomplished from the perspective of the eternal Word, even though the cross-and-resurrection still lay ahead historically. 'Be of good cheer' (tharseite — take courage, be confident) is therefore not consolation despite-defeat but participatory rejoicing-in-victory: the disciples are invited to share Christ's confidence that the outcome is settled. This grounds the Tewahedo martyrological tradition's characteristic theological confidence.
